extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of journalism, political scientists, publishers, and informed citizens
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for assessing the role, performance, and economic constraints of newspapers as sources of public information in a modern democracy. Emphasizes truth, the invisible environment, circulation economics, readership loyalty, and institutional checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper as provider of a true picture of the outer (invisible) world
rubrics_metrics.description: The press should daily 'present us with a true picture of all the outer world in which we are interested.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The truth about distant or complex matters is not self-evident; assembling that information is technical and expensive. The press is the chief means of contact with the unseen environment and thus bears the obligation to make that world visible to citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil liberty is necessary but not sufficient for public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil liberty (free speech, open encounter of opinions) is of fundamental practical value but 'does not guarantee public opinion in the modern world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free debate may vindicate truth over long time spans, but when dealing with complex/invisible matters, truth is not spontaneous and requires technical reporting and institutions beyond mere liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess government by concrete standards of living and results
rubrics_metrics.description: Political decision should be judged by whether government is producing 'a certain minimum of health, of decent housing, of material necessities, of education, of freedom, of pleasures, of beauty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift democratic faith from assuming instinctive good government to judging policy by measurable results; where criteria can be made exact and objective, decisions are brought into relation with citizens' interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insist on recording acts and objective measurement (audits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public control increases by 'insisting that all of them shall be plainly recorded, and their results objectively measured.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devising standards of living and methods of audit is a practical route to control officials and directors; work on such standards and audits has only begun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers are judged by community moral standards but operate under different economics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethically a newspaper is judged 'as if it were a church or a school' even though its economics (sold below cost, advertising-funded) differ from those institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers expect disinterestedness yet do not openly pay for news; this mismatch shapes both ethical expectations and the practical functioning of the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public expectation that news should be provided gratis
rubrics_metrics.description: The public 'does not think for a moment that he ought to pay for his newspaper' and treats news as if it should be free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although readers will pay for other services, they resist paying openly for news; instead payment is concealed via advertising and purchase of advertised goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation as the asset sold to advertisers
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation 'becomes an asset only when it can be sold to the advertiser' and the type of circulation (quality vs mass) depends on what advertisers want to sell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers target customers with discretionary income; papers reaching relatively prosperous homes are more valuable for general advertising. Circulation strategy therefore shapes editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for the buying public's point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: A press 'is bound to respect the point of view of the buying public' because alienating that public endangers the paper's existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers may attack powerful interests, but if they alienate the buying public they lose their indispensable asset; editors tailor content to avoid alienation of advertisers' customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate reader loyalty (constancy) as primary economic safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of every publisher is 'to turn his circulation ... into a devoted band of constant readers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loyal readers grant a paper independence from advertisers; subscription and habitual readership are more valuable than transient buyers. Loyalty depends on many subtle elements beyond pure newsgathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers judge newspapers by coverage of matters in which they are personally involved
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of us 'tends to judge a newspaper ... by its treatment of that part of the news in which we feel ourselves involved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the paper gives a satisfactory account of events within a reader's experience (business, church, party), it gains trust; this personal criterion often outweighs general-news accuracy for many readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local news is self-correcting; distant news lacks corrective mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Rarely is anyone but the interested party able to test accuracy; 'if the news is not local, the corrective diminishes as the subject matter recedes into the distance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-local reporting is harder to check and therefore more vulnerable to error or stereotyping; only organized groups can effectively correct distant misrepresentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal limitation on the general reader's remedies for misleading news
rubrics_metrics.description: The general reader 'has no standing in law if he thinks he is being misled by the news'; only aggrieved parties can sue for slander or libel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law assumes general news is not a matter of common concern except for moral or seditious content, so public remedies for inaccurate general reporting are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papers must diversify content to hold large audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers include features—'society, scandal and crime, sports, pictures, actresses, advice to the lovelorn ... cooking receipts, comic strips'—to hold readers who are not continually interested in political news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because big news alone cannot sustain mass circulation, editors add entertainment, local diaries, and specialty content to maintain readership and differentiate themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic pressures degrade reporting as a vocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting is 'the most poorly paid branch of newspaper work, and is the least regarded,' so able men treat reporting as temporary stage work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low pay and lack of strong professional traditions reduce recruitment and retention of talent in straight reporting, weakening standards and craft pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from advertisers increases with larger readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Axion: 'more readers, more independence of the influence of advertisers; fewer readers and more dependence on the advertiser.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large, loyal readership distributes advertiser influence and gives publishers leverage to resist advertiser dictation; small circulations are more vulnerable to advertiser pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique that ownership by Big Business corrupts truth in the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Upton Sinclair's thesis: owners and advertisers ('Big Business') prostitute truth; 'the fair body of truth would be inviolate in a press not in any way connected with Big Business.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a moral critique of economic control; the text notes that if an independent press still failed to contain truth, Sinclair's theory would be undermined—inviting scrutiny of both economic influence and other causes of error.
